result.family: enum and const equality semantics (Python `==` with a boolean-vs-number guard), Draft7Validator + ErrorTree

rules.rule: Output shape is invariant: exactly 10 lines = [treeTotal, n, n, B, B, B, "None", "None", treeTotal, treeTotal] where B is Python-style "True"/"False" (capitalized) and equals (n===0). Lines 2 and 3 are always identical (iter_errors is re-runnable, no generator exhaustion). Lines 1, 9, 10 are always identical. Lines 7,8 are the literal string "None" (check_schema returns None). Exit 0.
rules.evidence: --a '1' --b '{"allOf":[{"enum":[2]},{"enum":[3]}]}' -> `1 2 2 False False False None None 1 1` exit=0. Every non-crashing probe (100+) matched this shape.

rules.rule: Equality function `equal(a,b)` used by BOTH const and enum, applied recursively: (1) if a and b are the SAME OBJECT -> equal; (2) else if either is a string -> plain string equality (a string is never equal to an array/object even with the same elements); (3) else if both are arrays -> equal lengths AND element-wise equal(); (4) else if both are objects -> same key set AND value-wise equal(); (5) else compare unbool(a) == unbool(b), where unbool maps true/false to unique sentinels so a boolean is NEVER equal to any number.
Boolean/number guard is RECURSIVE, not just top-level. true !== 1, false !== 0 at any nesting depth, in both directions, for both enum and const.
rules.evidence: true|{"enum":[1]}->1 err; 1|{"enum":[true]}->1; false|{"enum":[0]}->1; 0|{"enum":[false]}->1; true|{"const":1}->1; 1|{"const":true}->1; [true]|{"const":[1]}->1; [1]|{"const":[true]}->1; {"a":true}|{"const":{"a":1}}->1; {"a":1}|{"const":{"a":true}}->1; [true]|{"enum":[[1]]}->1; [1]|{"enum":[[true]]}->1; [[true]]|{"enum":[[[1]]]}->1; {"a":{"b":true}}|{"enum":[{"a":{"b":1}}]}->1; 1.0|{"enum":[true]}->1; true|{"enum":[1.0]}->1; false|{"const":-0.0}->1; [0,1]|{"const":[false,true]}->1. All produce `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`.

rules.rule: true equals true and false equals false (unbool sentinels are stable). {"const":true} with true -> valid.
rules.evidence: true|{"const":true} -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; false|{"enum":[null,false]} -> 0 errors.

rules.rule: Numbers compare by mathematical value across int/float representations, with ARBITRARY-PRECISION integer semantics. Integer literals must be kept as exact big integers; do NOT coerce to IEEE double. int-vs-float comparison must be exact (compare the float's exact rational value against the big int).
Cross-type never equal: string vs number, string vs boolean, null vs anything else.
rules.evidence: '"1"'|{"enum":[1]}->1; 1|{"enum":["1"]}->1; '"1"'|{"const":1}->1; '"true"'|{"const":true}->1; true|{"const":"true"}->1; 1|{"const":null}->1; null|{"enum":[false,0]}->1; 0|{"enum":[null]}->1; null|{"const":null}->0; null|{"enum":[null]}->0.

rules.rule: Empty enum `{"enum":[]}` is a VALID Draft-7 schema (check_schema does NOT reject it; the draft-07 metaschema declares enum as {type:array, items:true} with no minItems/uniqueItems) and it makes every instance invalid with exactly 1 error.
rules.evidence: 1|{"enum":[]} -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; null|{"enum":[]} -> same; []|{"enum":[]} -> same; true|{"enum":[]} -> same. Exit 0 in all cases, so check_schema did not raise.

rules.rule: Duplicate enum entries are ALSO accepted by check_schema and behave as a plain membership test (no error, no dedup effect).
enum and const are independent keywords: both may be present and each yields its own error, producing 2 separate ErrorTree buckets (keywords "enum" and "const") at the same path.
rules.evidence: 1|{"const":2,"enum":[3]} -> `2 2 2 False False False None None 2 2`; 2|{"enum":[1,3],"const":3} -> 2 2 2 ...; 2|{"enum":[1,2,3],"const":2} -> 0 0 0 True...; 1|{"const":2,"not":{"const":1},"enum":[3]} -> `3 3 3 False False False None None 3 3` (keywords const/not/enum).

rules.rule: ErrorTree (line 1) groups by the pair (absolute instance path, error.validator keyword). Two errors sharing BOTH collapse into one; total = recursive sum over the path tree of the number of distinct keywords at each node. Line 2 is the raw error count.
Collapse is keyed on the FINAL instance path, so errors at different instance paths never collapse even with the same keyword; and sub-tree counts add up.

Keywords that transparently forward child errors to the parent's path — allOf, $ref, if/then/else, dependencies (schema form), patternProperties+properties overlapping the same property, propertyNames — all contribute errors whose keyword is the CHILD keyword and whose path is the descended path, so they can collapse with sibling errors. propertyNames errors keep the PARENT object's path (not the property name), so N bad property names collapse to 1.
anyOf / oneOf / not / contains collapse internally: they emit exactly ONE error at the parent path with their own keyword, never child errors. So they cannot collapse with an inner const/enum error.

Python's json parser is used, so it accepts NaN / Infinity / -Infinity literals in BOTH --a and --b, and it returns the SAME singleton float objects for them. Because equal() short-circuits on object identity, NaN EQUALS NaN under const/enum (contrary to IEEE), and NaN is of type "number".
rules.evidence: NaN|{"const":NaN} -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; NaN|{"enum":[NaN]} -> 0; [NaN]|{"const":[NaN]} -> 0; --a={"a":NaN} --b={"const":{"a":NaN}} -> 0; --a=NaN --b={"enum":[1,NaN]} -> 0; NaN|{"type":"number"} -> 0; NaN|{"const":1} -> 1 err; 1|{"const":NaN} -> 1 err. Infinity: Infinity|{"const":Infinity} -> 0; Infinity|{"const":1e400} -> 0; 1e400|{"const":Infinity} -> 0; 1e309|{"const":1e309} -> 0; --a=-Infinity --b={"const":-Infinity} -> 0; Infinity|{"const":-1e400} -> 1 err.

rules.rule: Boolean schemas are legal: schema `true` -> 0 errors/valid; schema `false` -> 1 error/invalid. Any other non-object top-level schema (null, string, array) CRASHES before any print.
rules.evidence: 1|true -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`; 1|false -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; 1|[] -> EMPTY exit=1 (AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get' in referencing/jsonschema.py _legacy_dollar_id); 1|null -> EMPTY exit=1 (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable); 1|'"enum"' -> EMPTY exit=1 (AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get').

rules.rule: A non-array `enum` value ALWAYS produces EMPTY/exit=1, but by two different mechanisms: number/null/boolean crash inside iter_errors (TypeError: '<type>' object is not iterable at jsonschema/_keywords.py:270), while string/object survive iter_errors (iterating chars/keys) and then crash in check_schema with SchemaError. Reimplementers can treat all of them uniformly as a hard failure.
rules.evidence: 1|{"enum":1} -> EMPTY exit=1, `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":null} -> `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":true} -> `TypeError: 'bool' object is not iterable`; 1|{"enum":"abc"} -> `jsonschema.exceptions.SchemaError: 'abc' is not of type 'array'` / `Failed validating 'type' in metaschema['properties']['enum']: {'type': 'array', 'items': True}`; '"a"'|{"enum":"abc"} -> same SchemaError even though "a" is a member of the chars; 1|{"enum":{"a":1}} -> SchemaError `{'a': 1} is not of type 'array'`.

rules.rule: `const` accepts ANY JSON value with no metaschema restriction (const: null, const: [], const: {} are all fine).
$schema in the schema does not change behavior: the validator is hard-wired to Draft 7 and check_schema always validates against the draft-07 metaschema.
rules.evidence: 1|{"$schema":"http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#","const":2} -> `1 1 1 False False False None None 1 1`; 1|{"$schema":"http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#","const":2} -> identical output.

rules.rule: Duplicate object keys in the input JSON are resolved last-wins by the parser before comparison.
rules.evidence: '{"a":1,"a":2}'|{"const":{"a":2}} -> `0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0`.

rules.rule: Strings compare by Unicode code points after JSON unescaping; no normalization.
rules.evidence: '"é"'|{"const":"é"} -> 0 0 0 True True True None None 0 0.

surprises: NaN == NaN is TRUE here. Python's json decoder returns one shared `float('nan')` singleton for every `NaN` literal, and jsonschema's equal() starts with an `a is b` identity check, so `--a NaN --b '{"const":NaN}'` validates (0 errors). A JS reimplementation using `===`/Object.is-free comparison would report invalid. Same for `[NaN]` vs const `[NaN]` and `{"a":NaN}` vs const `{"a":NaN}`.

JSON input accepts NaN, Infinity, -Infinity and out-of-range literals like 1e400 (-> Infinity). JSON.parse in JS rejects NaN/Infinity outright and silently maps 1e400 to Infinity. Note 1e400 === Infinity here (const:1e400 matches instance Infinity).

Integers are arbitrary precision. 10000000000000000001 !== 10000000000000000002 and 9007199254740993 !== 9007199254740992, but naive JSON.parse in JS collapses all of these to the same double. Must parse integer literals as BigInt (or compare literal text) to reproduce.

int-vs-float comparison is exact, not double-rounded: 1e19 == 10000000000000000000 (valid) but 1e19 != 10000000000000000001 (invalid), and 9007199254740993.0 != 9007199254740993 (the float literal rounds down to ...92). So the float side must be converted to its exact value, not the int side to a float.

Empty enum `[]` and duplicate enum entries are BOTH accepted by Draft-7 check_schema (draft-07 dropped minItems/uniqueItems from the enum metaschema). Many reimplementers assume check_schema rejects them. Empty enum just makes everything invalid with 1 error.

A string enum value (`{"enum":"abc"}`) does NOT crash iter_errors — it iterates characters — but still produces EMPTY output because check_schema raises later. Since all prints happen at the end, you cannot observe the partial success.

The boolean/number guard is recursive through arrays and objects, including inside enum members: `[1]` against `{"enum":[[true]]}` is INVALID. An older jsonschema used `instance not in enums` (Python list `==`), which would call that valid; this build does not.
-0.0 == 0 (valid) but false != -0.0 (the unbool guard beats numeric equality).
A string is never equal to an array of its characters: `"ab"` vs const `["a","b"]` is invalid in both directions.

ErrorTree collapse only requires (path, keyword) to match; the schema location is irrelevant. `{"const":2,"if":{"const":1},"then":{"const":3}}` gives 2 raw errors but treeTotal 1, and `{"dependencies":{"a":{"const":2}},"const":3}` likewise. propertyNames errors are filed under the parent object's path, so 2 bad key names collapse to 1.

argparse artifact: `--a '-Infinity'` fails with exit code 2 ("argument --a: expected one argument") because the value looks like a flag. `--a=-Infinity` works. `--a '-1'` works (looks like a negative number).

result.family: "type" keyword and the underlying type system (Draft7Validator + ErrorTree), test18_executable

rules.rule: Output shape is fixed: line1=ErrorTree.total_errors, line2=line3=raw len(iter_errors), lines4-6 = Python bool literal `True`/`False` (capital T/F) and always equal to (rawCount==0), lines7-8 = literal `None`, lines9-10 = same value as line1. Exit 0. Any exception anywhere => completely EMPTY stdout, exit 1 (argparse failures give exit 2).
rules.evidence: --a 1 --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0 EXIT=0 ; --a 1 --b '{"type":"null"}' -> 1,1,1,False,False,False,None,None,1,1 EXIT=0

rules.rule: A failing `type` keyword produces EXACTLY ONE error at that instance node, regardless of how many type names are listed in the array.
rules.evidence: --a '{}' --b '{"type":["string","number","boolean","null","array","integer"]}' -> 1,1,1,False,False,False,None,None,1,1 ; --a '{}' --b '{"type":["string","number","boolean"]}' -> 1,1,1,...

rules.rule: Type membership table (instance -> which of the 7 names it satisfies): null->null; true/false->boolean ONLY (never number, never integer); JSON object->object; JSON array->array; string->string; int literal->number AND integer; float literal->number, and ALSO integer iff its float value has zero fractional part.
rules.evidence: --a true --b '{"type":"number"}' -> 1,1,1,False,... ; --a true --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 1,1,1,False,... ; --a 1.0 --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 0,0,0,True,... ; --a 2.0 --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 0,...,True ; --a 1.5 --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 1,1,1,False,...

rules.rule: Draft7 zero-fraction rule details: -0.0, 1e2, 1.0e0, 1e308 are all `integer`. 0.1 and -1.5 are not. 1.00000000000000001 and 1.0000000000000000000000001 ARE integer (they round to 1.0 in float64, so test the PARSED double, not the source text).

Overflowing float literals become Infinity: 1e400 / -1e400 / Infinity / -Infinity are `number` but NOT `integer`. NaN is `number` but NOT `integer`. (Python json.loads accepts the bare tokens NaN, Infinity, -Infinity — a strict JSON.parse in JS will throw instead; you must special-case these tokens.)
rules.evidence: --a 1e400 --b '{"type":"number"}' -> 0,...,True ; --a 1e400 --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 1,1,1,False ; --a NaN --b '{"type":"number"}' -> True ; --a NaN --b '{"type":"integer"}' -> 1,1,1,False ; --a=-Infinity --b '{"type":"number"}' -> 0,...,True

rules.rule: Integers are arbitrary precision and EXACT — no float64 rounding. Comparisons (const/enum/maximum) on >2^53 integers must be done with BigInt/decimal-string semantics in JS.

ErrorTree collapse key = (absolute instance path, validator keyword). Two errors sharing BOTH collapse into one; different keyword at the same path does NOT collapse. total_errors is computed recursively: node.total = (#distinct keywords among errors whose remaining path is empty at this node) + sum(child.total).
rules.evidence: COLLAPSE: --a null --b '{"allOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"}]}' -> 1,2,2,False,False,False,None,None,1,1 ; --a null --b '{"allOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"},{"type":"array"}]}' -> 1,3,3,...,1,1 ; NO COLLAPSE (different keywords): --a 3 --b '{"type":"string","enum":[1,2]}' -> 2,2,2,... ; RECURSIVE SUM: --a '{"a":1,"b":1}' --b '{"allOf":[{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"},"b":{"type":"string"}}},{"properties":{"a":{"type":"boolean"},"b":{"type":"boolean"}}}]}' -> 2,4,4,False,False,False,None,None,2,2

rules.rule: More confirmed line1<line2 (collapse) generators, all reducing N same-path same-keyword errors to 1: root `type` + allOf types; properties+patternProperties both hitting the same key with the same keyword; $ref merged with a sibling keyword under allOf; propertyNames with several bad names; dependencies array with several missing props; nested items+allOf.
rules.evidence: --a 1 --b '{"type":"string","allOf":[{"type":"boolean"},{"type":"array"}]}' -> 1,3,3,...,1,1 ; --a '{"a":1}' --b '{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"patternProperties":{"^a":{"type":"boolean"}}}' -> 1,2,2,...,1,1 (but with `{"enum":[9]}` instead of the boolean type -> 2,2,2,...,2,2) ; --a '{"aa":1,"bb":2}' --b '{"propertyNames":{"maxLength":1}}' -> 1,2,2,...,1,1 ; --a '{"a":1}' --b '{"dependencies":{"a":["b","c"]}}' -> 1,2,2,...,1,1 ; --a '[[1]]' --b '{"items":{"allOf":[{"items":{"type":"string"}},{"items":{"type":"boolean"}}]}}' -> 1,2,2,...,1,1 ; --a '{"a":1}' --b '{"allOf":[{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}}},{"properties":{"a":{"type":"boolean"}}}]}' -> 1,2,2,...,1,1

rules.rule: anyOf / oneOf / not / contains / if-then wrap their sub-errors: they emit exactly ONE error at the parent node (children are not surfaced by iter_errors), so no collapse and count is 1.
rules.evidence: --a null --b '{"anyOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"}]}' -> 1,1,1,... ; --a null --b '{"oneOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"string"}]}' -> 1,1,1,... ; --a '"x"' --b '{"oneOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"string"}]}' -> 1,1,1,False (2 matches = oneOf failure) ; --a '[1,2]' --b '{"contains":{"type":"string"}}' -> 1,1,1,... ; --a 1 --b '{"if":{"type":"integer"},"then":{"type":"string"}}' -> 1,1,1,...

rules.rule: allOf and $ref do NOT wrap: their sub-errors are surfaced individually with the parent's instance path, which is the main source of collapse.
rules.evidence: --a 1 --b '{"allOf":[{"$ref":"#/definitions/s"},{"type":"boolean"}],"definitions":{"s":{"type":"string"}}}' -> 1,2,2,False,False,False,None,None,1,1

rules.rule: `type` MUST be either a simpleType string or a non-empty array of UNIQUE simpleType strings, ANYWHERE in the schema (including unreached subschemas, `definitions`, and `not`). Otherwise check_schema raises SchemaError => EMPTY, exit 1. Legal names are exactly: null, boolean, object, array, number, string, integer (case-sensitive, no surrounding whitespace).
rules.evidence: '{"type":[]}' -> EMPTY exit=1 (SchemaError: [] is not valid under any of the given schemas, metaschema['properties']['type'] minItems 1) ; '{"type":["integer","integer"]}' -> EMPTY exit=1 (uniqueItems) ; '{"type":"Integer"}', '{"type":"int"}', '{"type":"NUMBER"}', '{"type":"integer "}', '{"type":" integer"}', '{"type":{}}' -> EMPTY exit=1 ; --a 1 --b '{"type":"integer","definitions":{"x":{"type":"int"}}}' -> EMPTY exit=1 ; --a 1 --b '{"type":"integer","not":{"type":"int"}}' -> EMPTY exit=1

rules.rule: `type` as a non-string, non-list scalar (number / null / true / false) crashes EARLIER, at iter_errors, with TypeError "'X' object is not iterable" (jsonschema/_keywords.py line 285) — still EMPTY exit 1. `type` as an object {} is iterated over its KEYS instead (dict is iterable), so it does not TypeError; it fails later at check_schema.
rules.evidence: --a 1 --b '{"type":1}' -> EMPTY exit=1, stderr: File jsonschema/_keywords.py line 285 in type / TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable ; '{"type":null}' -> TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable ; '{"type":true}' -> TypeError: 'bool' object is not iterable ; '{"type":{}}' -> SchemaError at validators.py line 317 check_schema

rules.rule: Evaluation ORDER is observable: iter_errors runs BEFORE check_schema (test18.py line 17 vs line 33). The unknown-type lookup inside `type` is a short-circuiting any(), so an unknown type name only raises UnknownType at iter_errors if it is actually REACHED (i.e. no earlier listed name matched the instance). Otherwise the SchemaError from check_schema fires instead. Both give EMPTY exit 1, so the distinction is only visible on stderr — a JS reimplementation can treat all invalid `type` as exit 1.
rules.evidence: --a '"x"' --b '{"type":["string","int"]}' -> EMPTY exit=1, stderr: test18.py line 33 -> validators.py:317 check_schema -> SchemaError ; --a 1 --b '{"type":["string","int"]}' -> EMPTY exit=1, stderr: _keywords.py:285 -> UnknownType: Unknown type 'int' ; --a '"x"' --b '{"type":["int","string"]}' -> UnknownType (int checked first)

rules.rule: Sibling keywords are applied INDEPENDENTLY of a failing `type`; a type error does not suppress other keyword errors at the same node. Each applicable keyword adds its own error.
rules.evidence: --a '"abc"' --b '{"type":"integer","minLength":10}' -> 2,2,2,False,... ; --a '[1]' --b '{"type":"object","minItems":5}' -> 2,2,2,... ; --a '{"a":1}' --b '{"type":"array","required":["b"],"minProperties":5}' -> 3,3,3,...

rules.rule: Each keyword self-gates on the instance's type and silently passes for non-applicable types. Booleans are exempt from ALL numeric keywords (they are not `number`).
rules.evidence: --a true --b '{"exclusiveMinimum":5,"multipleOf":2,"maximum":0}' -> 0,0,0,True,... ; --a true --b '{"maxLength":0,"minLength":3,"pattern":"^z$"}' -> True ; --a true --b '{"minItems":3,"maxItems":0,"uniqueItems":true}' -> True ; --a true --b '{"required":["a"],"minProperties":2}' -> True ; --a 1 --b '{"maxLength":0,"minItems":5,"required":["a"]}' -> True ; --a '"abc"' --b '{"minimum":5,"minItems":5,"required":["a"]}' -> True

rules.rule: Equality for const/enum/uniqueItems: 1 == 1.0 (numeric equality, cross int/float), but booleans are NEVER equal to numbers, at any nesting depth (special bool-vs-number guard in the deep comparison).

rules.rule: String length is measured in Unicode CODE POINTS (Python semantics), not UTF-16 units. An astral character counts as 1.

rules.rule: Schema must be a JSON object or a JSON boolean. `true` = always valid, `false` = 1 error at the node. Any other top-level schema JSON (array, null, string, number) crashes during Draft7Validator construction/first use with AttributeError/TypeError from referencing/_legacy_dollar_id => EMPTY exit 1.

rules.rule: Unknown/misspelled keywords are ignored (no error, no schema error). Keyword names are case-sensitive.

rules.rule: `$schema` is ignored for dialect selection — Draft-7 semantics and the Draft-7 metaschema are always used, even for a draft-04 or bogus $schema value. Consequently draft-04-only forms like boolean `exclusiveMinimum` are a SchemaError.

rules.rule: Instance JSON parsing uses Python json.loads: duplicate object keys -> last one wins; leading/trailing whitespace OK; lone surrogates in \uXXXX escapes are accepted; but leading zeros (01), single quotes, `undefined`, and empty string are parse errors => EMPTY exit 1.

surprises: `1.0` IS an `integer` in Draft 7 (any float with zero fractional part), including -0.0, 1e2, 1e308, and 1.00000000000000001 (which rounds to 1.0). A naive JS `Number.isInteger` check on the raw token, or a 'has a decimal point => not integer' rule, gets this wrong.

`1e400` and `NaN` are `number` but NOT `integer` (they become inf/nan and fail is_integer). Also, Python json.loads ACCEPTS the bare tokens NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, which strict JSON.parse in JS rejects.

Booleans are never `number`/`integer`, AND they are exempt from every numeric/string/array/object keyword — `true` validates clean against {"minimum":5,"multipleOf":2,"maxLength":0,"minItems":3,"required":["a"]}.

Integers are arbitrary precision: 10000000000000000001 != 10000000000000000000 and 9007199254740993 != 9007199254740992. JS Number collapses both pairs, so const/enum/maximum comparisons need BigInt or string-based comparison.

ErrorTree collapses by (path, keyword): {"allOf":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"},{"type":"array"}]} on null gives line1=1 but line2=3. allOf and $ref surface child errors at the parent path (collapsible); anyOf/oneOf/not/contains/if-then wrap into a single parent error (never collapsible).

An unknown type NAME anywhere in the schema — even in `definitions` or inside a `not` that is logically irrelevant — kills the whole run (exit 1), because check_schema validates the entire schema against the Draft-7 metaschema. But whether the failure comes from iter_errors (UnknownType) or check_schema (SchemaError) depends on the short-circuiting any(): {"type":["string","int"]} raises UnknownType for instance 1 and SchemaError for instance "x".

`type` values that are ints/null/bools crash with TypeError 'not iterable' inside the type keyword BEFORE check_schema, while `type: {}` does not (a dict is iterable over its keys) and instead fails at check_schema. Duplicate entries ({"type":["integer","integer"]}) and empty arrays ({"type":[]}) are metaschema violations, not validation failures.
String lengths are code points, so "😀" satisfies {"maxLength":1} and violates {"minLength":2}; JS `.length` gives 2 and inverts both results.
A top-level schema of `[]`, `null`, `"x"`, or `1` crashes at validator construction (referencing/_legacy_dollar_id), not at validation — but `true`/`false` are perfectly valid boolean schemas.

Python `$` semantics: `$` matches at end of string OR immediately before a single trailing '\n'. It does NOT match before '\r' or before '\r\n', and does not match before a second trailing newline.

rules.rule: Python `^` is start-of-string only (no /m by default); `.` does not match '\n' but DOES match '\r'. Inline flags (?s), (?m), (?x), (?a), (?i) work but ONLY at the very start of the pattern — a mid-pattern global flag is a re.error and crashes.

rules.rule: \d, \w, \s are FULL-UNICODE by default (Python str patterns are re.UNICODE). \d matches Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits, \w matches accented letters, \s matches NBSP and EM SPACE. (?a) restores ASCII-only. JS \d/\w are ASCII-only, so a translator must expand these classes.
Regex operates on CODE POINTS: '.' matches a whole astral character and a character class may contain an astral literal. Equivalent to JS RegExp with the /u flag.
(?i) uses Python's Unicode simple case folding: 'K' (U+212A KELVIN SIGN) matches /k/i, but 'ß' does NOT match 'ss'.

Python-only regex syntax that must be supported: named group (?P<x>...), backreference (?P=x), numeric backreference \1, conditional (?(1)a|b), comment group (?#...), \A, \Z, bare ']' and bare '{' as literals, POSIX-looking [[:alpha:]] treated as an ordinary character class (NOT a POSIX class), and possessive quantifiers a*+ (Python 3.11+).

Syntax that is a re.error in Python (=> EMPTY, exit 1) even though JS accepts some of it: JS-style named group (?<x>...), \z, \g<1>, \Q...\E, \p{L}, variable-width lookbehind, atomic group (?>...) is accepted-but-different, leading '*', 'a**', unterminated '[' or '('.

'{"pattern":"(a)\\g<1>"}' -> bad escape \g at position 3. '{"pattern":"\\Qa\\E"}' -> bad escape \Q. '{"pattern":"\\p{L}"}' -> bad escape \p at position 0. '{"pattern":"(?<=x*)a"}' -> look-behind requires fixed-width pattern. '{"pattern":"*a"}' -> nothing to repeat. '{"pattern":"a**"}' -> multiple repeat at position 2. '{"pattern":"["}' -> unterminated character set. Atomic group '(?>a*)ab' on '"aab"' -> 1,1,1,False,... (no backtracking, so no match).

Python `$` matches before a single trailing newline: pattern '^abc$' VALIDATES the string "abc

\d, \w, \s are Unicode-aware: '٣' and '１' match ^\d$, 'é' matches ^\w$, NBSP/EM-SPACE match ^\s$. A naive JS port using the same source string gets all four backwards.

`format` is completely inert during validation (no format_checker), yet check_schema DOES enforce format 'regex' on `pattern` values and `patternProperties` keys. So {"format":"email"} never errors, but {"pattern":"["} kills the whole program.

An invalid regex ANYWHERE in the schema — including inside `definitions` or a branch the instance never reaches, and even when the instance is a number — aborts everything with empty stdout and exit 1, because check_schema walks the entire schema.
Non-integer/negative/boolean minLength (3.5, -1, true) crash via check_schema, but integer-valued floats (3.0, 1e2) are perfectly legal and behave as integers.
A STRING minLength value crashes only if the instance is a string (TypeError inside the keyword), otherwise it crashes later inside check_schema — different traceback, identical observable output.
[[:alpha:]] is NOT a POSIX class in Python; it is a character class of the literals [ : a l p h and does not match 'a'.
Python-only regex constructs like (?P<x>...), (?P=x), (?(1)a|b), (?#...), \A, \Z, and possessive a*+ are legal; JS-only forms (?<x>...), \z, \g<1>, \p{L}, variable-width lookbehind are hard errors.
Mid-pattern global inline flags such as 'a(?i)bc' are a re.error in modern Python, so they crash instead of validating.
(?>a*)ab is an atomic group in Python 3.11+ and therefore does NOT match "aab" (1 error), unlike a plain (a*)ab which would.
Schema values `true`/`false` are valid schemas, but `null`, a string, or an array as the schema crash with AttributeError/TypeError.

rules.rule: ErrorTree collapse key = (absolute instance path tuple, error.validator keyword). Two top-level errors with the SAME path AND SAME keyword count once in line1; different keyword OR different path count separately. total_errors = sum over all tree nodes of (number of distinct keywords at that node).

(same path '', same keyword 'minimum'); --a '"abcd"' --b '{"allOf":[{"minLength":10},{"maxLength":1}]}' -> 2,2,2 (different keywords); --a '{"a":5,"b":5}' --b '{"properties":{"a":{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20}]},"b":{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20}]}}}' -> 2,4,4 (two paths x collapse)

rules.rule: anyOf: if ANY branch validates, 0 errors. If ALL branches fail, exactly ONE error is emitted, with validator keyword "anyOf" and path = the instance path of the anyOf keyword. Sub-branch errors are NOT emitted at top level (they live only in .context). Number of branches is irrelevant to the count.
rules.evidence: --a 5 --b '{"anyOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20},{"minimum":30}]}' -> 1,1,1,...; --a 5 --b '{"anyOf":[{"type":"string"},{"maxLength":1}]}' -> 0,0,0 (maxLength vacuously passes on a number)

rules.rule: oneOf: exactly one match -> 0 errors. Zero matches -> exactly 1 error, keyword "oneOf". Two or more matches -> exactly 1 error, also keyword "oneOf" ("is valid under each of ..."). Never more than 1 error from a single oneOf.
rules.evidence: --a 15 --b '{"oneOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20}]}' -> 0,0,0; --a 5 --b same -> 1,1,1; --a 25 --b same -> 1,1,1 (two match); --a 35 --b '{"oneOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20},{"minimum":30}]}' -> 1,1,1 (three match)

rules.rule: allOf: does NOT wrap. Every sub-error of every branch is emitted individually at top level, carrying the SUB-schema's keyword and the sub-error's instance path. Count = sum over branches of that branch's error count.
rules.evidence: --a 5 --b '{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20},{"minimum":30}]}' -> 1,3,3,... (3 raw, collapse to 1); --a 5 --b '{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"maxLength":1}]}' -> 1,1,1 (maxLength doesn't apply to numbers)

rules.rule: allOf nesting is flattened for counting: nested allOf sub-errors still surface individually with the innermost keyword and root path.
not: instance valid against the subschema -> exactly 1 error with keyword "not"; invalid -> 0 errors. Subschema errors never surface. `not:{}` and `not:true` always fail; `not:false` always passes.
Two `not` errors at the same path collapse in the tree (same keyword "not").

if/then/else: `if` is evaluated silently (its own errors are never emitted). If `if` passes -> descend into `then` (if present); if `if` fails -> descend into `else` (if present). Errors from then/else are emitted individually with the SUB-schema's keyword (NOT "then"/"else"/"if"), exactly like allOf. So a `then` error with keyword `minimum` COLLAPSES with a sibling root-level `minimum` error.

rules.rule: if with no then and no else -> always 0 errors, regardless of whether `if` matches. `then`/`else` WITHOUT `if` are completely ignored (not even schema-descended at validation time).

if/then/else full truth table (instance 5): if passes + then fails -> then's errors; if passes + else fails -> 0 (else skipped); if fails + then fails -> 0 (then skipped); if fails + else fails -> else's errors. `if:true` always takes the then branch, `if:false` always takes the else branch.

allOf does NOT produce a single wrapper error — it leaks every sub-error individually (line2 grows), while anyOf/oneOf/not produce exactly ONE error each no matter how many branches or sub-errors exist. This asymmetry is the main driver of line1 != line2.
oneOf with TWO OR MORE matching branches is an ERROR (1 error, keyword "oneOf") — easy to forget; and it is still just 1 error, same as zero matches.
Boolean subschema `false` errors have validator = None, so `{"allOf":[false,false]}` collapses to tree=1 while `{"allOf":[false,{"minimum":10}]}` stays at 2.
`then`/`else` present WITHOUT `if` are completely inert (0 errors) — but they are still metaschema-checked, so `{"then":[]}` still crashes at check_schema.
`if` failing with only a `then` present yields 0 errors (the else branch is absent), and `if` passing with only `else` present also yields 0 errors.

Draft7 `$ref` suppresses ALL sibling keywords in the same schema object, including allOf/anyOf/if — `{"$ref":"#/d","allOf":[...]}` ignores the allOf entirely.
`required:["b","c"]` emits TWO errors (one per missing property) that then collapse to one tree entry — another raw!=tree source unrelated to combinators.
Line 7 and 8 print the literal string `None` (check_schema returns None on success), never `True`.

rules.rule: CORE ALGORITHM (confirmed): build a tree of nodes. Each node has `errors` = dict keyword->error and `contents` = dict pathElement->childNode (auto-created on access). For each error e in iter_errors order: cur = root; for each element in e.absolutePath: cur = cur.contents[element] (creating if absent); then cur.errors[e.keyword] = e (OVERWRITES). total_errors = size(node.errors) + sum(child.total_errors) recursively. So two errors sharing (absolute instance path, keyword) collapse to 1; anything differing in either stays separate.

(tree 1, raw 4). same path+diff keyword: --a '5' --b '{"minimum":10,"multipleOf":7}' -> 2|2|2. diff path+same keyword: --a '{"a":1,"b":2}' --b '{"properties":{"a":{"type":"string"},"b":{"type":"string"}}}' -> 2|2|2.

rules.rule: Collapse is by keyword only, regardless of which schema location produced the error. Two `minimum` errors at the same path from two different allOf branches collapse; two `type` errors at path ['a'] from two allOf branches collapse.

A boolean `false` schema produces one error whose keyword is None/null. Two such errors at the same path collapse into ONE tree entry (None collides with None), but None does not collide with any real keyword, so `false` + a real error at the same path gives tree 2.

allOf / $ref / if-then / if-else / dependencies(schema form) are TRANSPARENT: the sub-schema's own keywords and the parent's instance path are what land in the tree (no 'allOf'/'$ref'/'then'/'dependencies' keyword is used).

`propertyNames` errors keep the OBJECT's path (the property name is NOT appended). N failing property names x M failing keywords in the propertyNames subschema => raw N*M, tree M.

surprises: ErrorTree construction can CRASH the whole program. `ErrorTree.__getitem__` probes `node.instance[element]` as a guard whenever it descends into a not-yet-existing child, and a propertyNames error leaves node.instance set to the offending property NAME (a string). Indexing a string with a string raises TypeError, so a perfectly legal schema+instance pair yields EMPTY stdout / exit 1. A naive reimplementation would happily print counts.

That crash is sensitive to JSON OBJECT KEY ORDER in the schema. {"propertyNames":...,"properties":...} crashes; {"properties":...,"propertyNames":...} prints 2|2|2. Any reimplementation that uses an order-insensitive schema representation (or sorts keys) will diverge. You must preserve schema key insertion order and emit errors in that order.
Errors collapse by keyword regardless of origin: two `minimum` errors from two different allOf branches at the same path become ONE tree entry. Collapsing is not per-schema-location.

`required` with N missing props emits N raw errors but 1 tree entry; `dependencies` (array form) does the same. `additionalProperties: false` conversely emits only ONE raw error no matter how many extras.
`propertyNames` errors do NOT extend the instance path with the property name — they stay at the object's path, so N bad names collapse to 1 per keyword.
A boolean `false` schema produces an error whose keyword is None/null; two None-keyword errors at the same path collapse with each other (allOf:[false,false] -> raw 2, tree 1).

anyOf/oneOf/not/contains contribute exactly one error each and their sub-errors (in .context) are invisible to the tree, while allOf/$ref/if-then/else/dependencies(schema) are fully transparent and contribute the sub-keywords directly.

Booleans are excluded from numeric keywords (true vs {"minimum":0,"maximum":0} is VALID) yet are distinguished from 1 by enum/const, and NOT distinguished by uniqueItems ([1,true] is unique-OK, [0,false] is unique-OK). JS with === / JSON.stringify gets several of these backwards.

check_schema runs after iter_errors, so which exception you see depends on whether the instance exercised the malformed keyword ({"pattern":"["} gives re.error for a string instance, SchemaError for a number instance) — but either way stdout is empty and exit is 1.
Self-referential $ref ({"$ref":"#/definitions/n","definitions":{"n":{"$ref":"#/definitions/n"}}}) blows the Python stack (RecursionError) rather than being detected.
Unknown `type` values raise UnknownType at validation time (exit 1) rather than being reported as a schema error, even though check_schema would also have flagged nothing for it.
Exit code 2 (argparse) must be distinguished from exit code 1 (any Python exception); both produce empty stdout.

result.family: numeric keywords: multipleOf, maximum, minimum, exclusiveMaximum, exclusiveMinimum (Draft7Validator + ErrorTree, test18_executable)

rules.rule: All five numeric keywords are type-gated: if the instance is not a Python 'number' the keyword returns immediately with no error AND no evaluation of the schema value. Python 'number' EXCLUDES booleans. So instance true/false/null/string/array/object => 0 errors for any numeric keyword, even a nonsensical or crashing one.
rules.evidence: --a 'true' --b '{"multipleOf": 2}' -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0 (EXIT=0). Same 10 lines for a=false, null, "7", [1], {"x":1} against {"multipleOf":2}, {"minimum":5}, {"exclusiveMaximum":3}. Decisive: --a '"a"' --b '{"multipleOf": NaN}' -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0 while --a '5' --b '{"multipleOf": NaN}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1 ValueError.

rules.rule: Comparison operators are exactly: minimum fails when instance < m; maximum fails when instance > M; exclusiveMinimum fails when instance <= m; exclusiveMaximum fails when instance >= M. (Confirmed by the operator named in the TypeError.)
rules.evidence: --a '5' --b '{"minimum": "5"}' -> TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'. {"maximum":"5"} -> '>'. {"exclusiveMinimum":"5"} -> '<='. {"exclusiveMaximum":"5"} -> '>='. Behaviourally: a=5,b={"minimum":5} -> 0 errors; a=5,b={"exclusiveMinimum":5} -> 1 error; a=5,b={"exclusiveMaximum":5} -> 1 error.

rules.rule: multipleOf has TWO completely different algorithms selected by the RUNTIME TYPE of the schema value (Python float vs int), i.e. by whether the JSON literal contained '.', 'e'/'E'. If the divisor token is a float literal: quotient = instance / dB (IEEE double division), fail iff int(quotient) != quotient. If the divisor token is an int literal: fail iff (instance % dB) is truthy (Python %, exact bigint arithmetic when both are ints).
rules.evidence: a=1e17 b={"multipleOf":3.0} -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0 (VALID) but a=1e17 b={"multipleOf":3} -> 1,1,1,False,... (INVALID). a=9007199254740993 b={"multipleOf":3.0} -> INVALID(1) but b={"multipleOf":3} -> VALID(0). a=1e18 b={"multipleOf":7.0}->VALID, b={"multipleOf":7}->INVALID. a=12345678901234567890123 b=7.0->VALID, b=7->INVALID. a=1e308 b=3.0->VALID, b=3->INVALID.

rules.rule: Consequence of the float-divisor rule: once |instance/dB| >= 2^53 the quotient double is always integral, so the check trivially PASSES. A JS reimplementation must reproduce int(q)!=q on the double quotient, not a tolerance/epsilon comparison.
Consequence #2 of the float-divisor rule: if the quotient UNDERFLOWS to 0.0 the check PASSES (0.0 is integral). Any tiny instance with a huge float divisor is a 'multiple'.
rules.evidence: a=5e-324 b={"multipleOf":1e300} -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0. a=5e-324 b={"multipleOf":1e308} -> VALID. a=1e-300 b={"multipleOf":1e300} -> VALID. Contrast a=5e-324 b={"multipleOf":2} (int divisor, 5e-324 % 2 = 5e-324 truthy) -> 1,1,1,False,...

rules.rule: multipleOf float-divisor path has an `except OverflowError` fallback that redoes the test in EXACT RATIONAL arithmetic (Fraction). It triggers when instance/dB overflows to inf so int(inf) raises. Rule: if the double quotient is +/-inf, decide validity by exact rational divisibility of the exact binary values of instance and dB.
rules.evidence: a=1e308 b={"multipleOf":5e-324} -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0 (VALID: 1e308 is an exact integer multiple of 2^-1074). a=1.0 b={"multipleOf":5e-324} -> VALID. a=2.0 and a=3.0 with 5e-324 -> VALID. a=1e308 b={"multipleOf":1.5e-323} (=3*2^-1074) -> 1 error (not divisible by 3). a=1e308 b={"multipleOf":1e-308} -> 1 error. a=1e308 b={"multipleOf":1e-300} -> 1 error. A naive impl returning 'invalid on inf quotient' gets the 5e-324 cases wrong.

rules.rule: The Fraction fallback itself raises (uncaught) when the instance or divisor is non-finite: quotient inf with a non-finite operand => chained OverflowError 'cannot convert Infinity to integer ratio' => EMPTY stdout, exit 1.
rules.evidence: --a '1e400' --b '{"multipleOf": 2.0}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1, stderr shows 'OverflowError: cannot convert float infinity to integer' then 'OverflowError: cannot convert Infinity to integer ratio'. Same for --a 'Infinity' --b '{"multipleOf": 2.0}' and --a=-1e400 --b '{"multipleOf":2.0}'.

rules.rule: `quotient = instance / dB` is OUTSIDE the try/except. So a Python bigint instance (JSON integer too large for a double) with ANY float divisor raises an uncaught OverflowError: 'int too large to convert to float' => EMPTY, exit 1. Same for a float instance with a bigint divisor (float % bigint).
rules.evidence: --a '1000...0' (10**400, 401 digits) --b '{"multipleOf": 1.5}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1 'OverflowError: int too large to convert to float'. --a '5.0' --b '{"multipleOf": 10**400}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1 same OverflowError. But --a '10**400' --b '{"multipleOf": 3}' -> 1,1,1,False,... (exact bigint modulo, no crash) and --b '{"multipleOf": 2}' -> 0 errors. And --a '5' --b '{"multipleOf": 10**400}' -> 1 error (int%int fine).

rules.rule: multipleOf 0 / 0.0 with a NUMBER instance raises ZeroDivisionError during iter_errors, BEFORE check_schema runs. Message differs by divisor type: int 0 -> 'integer modulo by zero'; float 0.0 -> 'float division by zero'. Both EMPTY exit 1.
rules.evidence: --a '10' --b '{"multipleOf": 0}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1 'ZeroDivisionError: integer modulo by zero'. --a '10' --b '{"multipleOf": 0.0}' -> EMPTY EXIT=1 'ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero'. --a '0' --b '{"multipleOf": 0}' -> same integer-modulo error.

rules.rule: Execution order is: json.loads(a) -> json.loads(b) -> Draft7Validator(schema) -> iter_errors (instance validation) -> ... -> check_schema LAST. Therefore an instance-validation exception (TypeError/ZeroDivisionError/ValueError/OverflowError) always wins over SchemaError; SchemaError only surfaces when instance validation completed cleanly (typically because the type gate skipped the keyword).
rules.evidence: --a '5' --b '{"minimum": "5"}' -> TypeError (not SchemaError). --a '"a"' --b '{"minimum": "5"}' -> jsonschema.exceptions.SchemaError: '5' is not of type 'number'. --a '10' --b '{"multipleOf": 0}' -> ZeroDivisionError; --a 'true' --b '{"multipleOf": 0}' -> SchemaError: 0 is less than or equal to the minimum of 0.

rules.rule: Because check_schema always runs, ANY schema failing the Draft7 metaschema produces EMPTY/exit 1 even when the instance validated fine. Metaschema constraints for this family: minimum/maximum/exclusiveMinimum/exclusiveMaximum must be type 'number'; multipleOf must be type 'number' AND exclusiveMinimum 0 (i.e. must satisfy NOT(value <= 0)).

rules.rule: A BOOLEAN schema value for a numeric keyword never raises TypeError during validation (Python bool IS int, so 5 < True and 5 % True work); it always dies later at check_schema with SchemaError 'True/False is not of type number'.

Contrast --a '5' --b '{"minimum": null}' -> TypeError: '<' not supported between int and NoneType, and --a '5' --b '{"minimum": [1]}' -> TypeError ... int and list, --a '5' --b '{"maximum": {}}' -> TypeError ... int and dict, --a '5' --b '{"multipleOf": {}}' -> TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for %: 'int' and 'dict'.

rules.rule: Python's json.loads accepts NaN / Infinity / -Infinity bare literals in BOTH --a and --b, and JSON numeric overflow (1e400) becomes inf rather than an error. A JS reimplementation must extend JSON.parse for these tokens.
rules.evidence: --a 'NaN' --b '{"minimum":5}' -> 0,0,0,True,True,True,None,None,0,0. --a 'Infinity' --b '{"multipleOf":2}' -> 1,1,1,False,... --a '1e400' --b '{"maximum":5}' -> 1 error (inf > 5). --a '1e400' --b '{"minimum":5}' -> 0 errors. --a '5' --b '{"minimum": Infinity}' -> 1 error.

rules.rule: ErrorTree groups errors by (absolute instance path, error.validator keyword); duplicates collapse. total_errors = sum over nodes of the number of DISTINCT keywords at that node. Lines 1, 9, 10 are always this collapsed count; line 2 and 3 are always the raw iter_errors count. They differ whenever two errors share both path and keyword (e.g. allOf branches repeating the same numeric keyword).

Three branches: '{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20},{"minimum":30}]}' -> 1,3,3,...,1,1. Distinct keywords do NOT collapse: '{"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"maximum":1}]}' -> 2,2,2,...,2,2. '{"minimum":10,"multipleOf":3,"maximum":1,"exclusiveMinimum":100,"exclusiveMaximum":0}' with a=5 -> 5,5,5,...,5,5. Per-path: --a '[1,2]' --b '{"items":{"allOf":[{"minimum":5},{"minimum":7}]}}' -> 2,4,4,...,2,2. --a '[1,1,1]' --b '{"items":{"allOf":[{"minimum":9},{"minimum":8},{"maximum":0}]}}' -> 6,9,9,...,6,6. $ref duplicates also collapse: '{"allOf":[{"$ref":"#/definitions/n"},{"$ref":"#/definitions/n"}],"definitions":{"n":{"minimum":9}}}' with a=5 -> 1,2,2,...,1,1.

rules.rule: anyOf/oneOf/not wrapping numeric subschemas produce exactly ONE top-level error (keyword anyOf/oneOf/not), not the child errors, so no collapse effect there.

Int-literal divisor path uses Python's % semantics (sign follows the divisor, and -0.0 is falsy). Since a negative divisor is rejected by check_schema anyway, in practice: with a positive int divisor, fail iff instance % dB != 0 using Python floor-mod, which for floats equals JS ((x % d) + d) % d.

rules.rule: Ordinary decimal multipleOf cases follow double rounding of the quotient exactly. Notable pass/fail pairs to reproduce: 0.0075/0.0001 rounds to exactly 75.0 -> VALID; 0.0075/0.00001 -> 750.0000000000001 -> INVALID; 0.1/0.01 rounds to exactly 10.0 -> VALID; 0.3/0.1 = 2.9999999999999996 -> INVALID; 0.7/0.1 -> INVALID; 0.6/0.2 -> INVALID; 1.1/0.11 -> VALID; 4.5/1.5 = 3.0 -> VALID; 4.5/1.5000000000000002 -> INVALID.
Comparison keywords never overflow: Python compares a bigint instance to a float bound (and vice versa) exactly, no crash.
rules.evidence: --a '10**400' --b '{"minimum": 1.5}' -> 0 errors; --b '{"maximum": 1.5}' -> 1 error. --a '5.0' --b '{"minimum": 10**400}' -> 1,1,1,False,...,1,1 (no OverflowError, unlike the multipleOf path).

Using '--a=<value>' bypasses this entirely.

surprises: multipleOf 2 and multipleOf 2.0 are NOT equivalent. The int literal takes an exact modulo path; the float literal takes a double-division + integrality path. They disagree for any instance whose quotient reaches 2^53 (1e17 vs 3 vs 3.0; 9007199254740993 vs 3 vs 3.0 — the int path says VALID and the float path says INVALID there, the opposite direction from the 1e17 case). JS has no int/float distinction, so you MUST inspect the raw JSON token of the divisor (presence of '.', 'e', 'E' => float) to pick the branch.

multipleOf with a float divisor PASSES whenever the double quotient is >= 2^53 (always integral) or underflows to 0.0. So {"multipleOf": 1e300} validates 5e-324, and {"multipleOf": 3.0} validates 1e17.

There is an exact-rational (Fraction) fallback when the quotient overflows to inf. 1e308 IS a valid multiple of 5e-324 (exit 0, zero errors) because 5e-324 = 2^-1074 divides every double exactly. A reimplementation that returns 'invalid' on an infinite quotient gets this wrong; you need BigInt rational arithmetic over the exact binary expansions.

Booleans are not numbers: {"minimum": 5} against instance true yields ZERO errors, and multipleOf 0 against a boolean instance does NOT divide-by-zero — it survives to check_schema and dies with SchemaError instead of ZeroDivisionError.

Conversely, a boolean SCHEMA value never triggers a TypeError (Python bool subclasses int, so 5 < True and 5 % True evaluate fine); it only fails later at check_schema. null/list/dict schema values DO raise TypeError.

check_schema runs LAST, so an invalid schema still crashes even when validation succeeded — but any exception raised during iter_errors preempts it. Which exception you see (ZeroDivisionError vs TypeError vs SchemaError) therefore depends on the instance's type.

Python's json.loads accepts NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, and silently maps 1e400 to inf. NaN instances pass every comparison keyword; a NaN bound passes check_schema (NaN <= 0 is False) and makes minimum/maximum/exclusive* vacuously satisfied. NaN with a float multipleOf raises ValueError (uncatchable by the OverflowError handler) while NaN with an int multipleOf just reports 1 error.
multipleOf Infinity accepts every finite number (quotient 0.0), and passes the metaschema.

Big JSON integers stay exact bigints in Python: 12345678901234567890123 % 7 is exact, but 12345678901234567890123 / 7.0 overflows only if the integer exceeds ~1.8e308, in which case it raises an UNCAUGHT OverflowError (the try only wraps the int() call, not the division).
ErrorTree collapses errors sharing (path, keyword): {"allOf":[{"minimum":10},{"minimum":20},{"minimum":30}]} against 5 prints 1 on line 1 but 3 on lines 2-3.

surprises: `--a -Infinity` is an ARGPARSE ERROR (exit 2), not a JSON value, because `-Infinity` fails argparse's negative-number regex `^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$`. Same for `-1e5`, `-1e400`, `-1.`, `-NaN`, `--1`. But `-1`, `-1.5`, `-0.5`, `-.5`, `-12345678901234567890` ARE accepted as values. A naive parser that just takes the next token, or one that rejects every token starting with `-`, gets both halves wrong.

A token starting with `-` is also accepted as a value if it CONTAINS A SPACE (`--a '-1 2'`, `--a '- 1'`) or is exactly `-`. These are argparse's other two escape hatches beyond the negative-number regex.

argparse reports the missing-required error BEFORE the unrecognized-arguments error, so `--A 1 --b true` says `the following arguments are required: --a` and never mentions `--A`. Reimplementations that validate unknown flags first will produce the wrong stderr.

`--` stops option parsing but is ITSELF left in the extras list, so it always shows up in `unrecognized arguments: -- ...`. `--a 1 --b true --` is exit 2, not a successful run. (This is the Python 3.12.5+/3.13 argparse behavior; older argparse silently swallowed the first `--`.)

Long-option abbreviation is on: `--he` and `--hel` invoke help. Also `-h`/`--help` short-circuits before the required-arg check, so `-h --a` prints help with exit 0 rather than erroring on the dangling `--a`.

json.loads accepts `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity` (JSON.parse rejects all three), and rejects the lowercase `nan`/`inf`. It also silently turns `1e400` into +inf, and `1e400` then FAILS `type: integer` while `1.0` PASSES it (Python int-valued-float rule).

Two `NaN` tokens in one document are the same interned Python float object, so `[NaN,NaN]` VIOLATES `uniqueItems: true` even though NaN != NaN. JS's default deep-equal will call them unequal and report 0 errors.
String lengths are code points, not UTF-16 units: `"😀"` (one emoji) satisfies `maxLength: 1`. JS `.length` would say 2.
JSON whitespace is exactly ` \t\n\r`. `\f`, `\v`, U+00A0 and U+2028 are all rejected with `Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` — U+2028 in particular is a JS-specific gotcha.
Lone/unpaired surrogate escapes (`"\ud800"`, `"\udc00"`, `"\ud83dx"`) are accepted without error by json.loads.
A UTF-8 BOM produces a unique message no other decoder emits: `Unexpected UTF-8 BOM (decode using utf-8-sig): line 1 column 1 (char 0)`.

Conversely `{"type":"nope"}` and `{"type":1}` crash even earlier, inside iter_errors.

A schema that is a bare int/float/null crashes with TypeError while a bare string/array crashes with AttributeError — the two non-object non-boolean schema shapes give different exception types, both at validator construction time (before iter_errors).
